note: Difficulty ladders (E2a for the 17 skeleton capabilities, E2b for the 39 core capabilities): for each capability, the features that make its items harder, in order, each at a band on OpenPath's 1-8 scale and under one of the capability's band descriptors. Bands are expert estimates, not empirically calibrated. For review by English educators (D-4).

steps.feature: Adds -s, -ing or -ed with no change to the base (plays, jumped, playing).
Adds -es after s, x, ch or sh (boxes, watches).
Doubles the final consonant of a short one-syllable word (swimming, running).
Drops a silent e before a vowel suffix (making, hoping).
Changes y to i after a consonant (carried, cried, happiest).
Doubles in two-syllable words stressed on the last syllable (beginning, forgetting, occurred).
Does not double when the stress is on the first syllable (visited, opening).
Handles exceptions: -c to -ck (panicked, picnicking), ie to y (lying).
Very common everyday words (first 1,000).
Common everyday words (about the 2,000-word level).
Words common in everyday texts (about the 3,000-word level).
Less frequent words met in secondary-school reading.
General words typical of secondary-level texts.
Low-frequency, precise general words.
Rare words with precise meanings.
-ful, -ly and -er on very familiar words (helpful, teacher).
Chooses the noun, adjective or adverb form of a common word for its place (careful/carefully).
Forms nouns with -ness, -ment and -tion on common words (kindness, invitation).
Less regular derivations (decide → decision, able → ability).
Recognises how a suffix changes meaning (-able: questionable, affordable).
Irregular, abstract derivations (maintenance, pronunciation, explanation).
The meaning is stated or restated right next to the word.
A nearby synonym or result in the same sentence.
An example or contrast clue (unlike …, in contrast).
Clues spread across two or more sentences.
The meaning follows from a whole situation or a result described later.
Subtle or indirect clues, including irony and a less common sense of a familiar word.
a or an chosen by the first letter of a common singular noun.
a for first mention, the for something already mentioned; a before a job.
a or an chosen by sound, not letter (an hour, a university).
the for something unique or known to everyone (the sun).
No a/an with uncountable nouns (advice, information, furniture).
General statements and abstract nouns (Tigers are …; Honesty is …).
Articles with proper nouns (the Ganga, Mount Everest).
Present progressive for an action happening now.
Stative verbs (know, belong) are not used in the progressive.
Past progressive for a longer action interrupted by a past event.
Present perfect for an unfinished period; past simple for a finished time.
Present perfect with just, already and yet.
Past perfect for an earlier past event (By the time we arrived, …).
Perfect progressive forms in narratives (had been waiting).
Adds -s or -es for a he/she/it subject in the simple present.
Plural and irregular plural noun subjects (the children are).
Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb.
Agreement across a phrase between subject and verb (the box of pencils is).
Indefinite pronouns and each/every (Each of the students has).
either … or / neither … nor: agree with the nearer subject.
Inverted order and 'the number of' / 'a number of'.
Commas between items in a simple list.
Commas after yes/no, names and introductory words; none between subject and verb.
A comma after an introductory phrase or clause.
A pair of commas around non-essential information.
A comma before a conjunction joining two clauses; not a comma alone (splice).
No commas around defining clauses; avoids unnecessary commas.
Commas that change meaning, and commas with sentence transitions (However, …).
Two short statements separated by a full stop and capital letter.
Finds and fixes a fused sentence (no punctuation between clauses).
Recognises a comma splice and a correct join with a conjunction.
Repairs run-ons with a conjunction or subordination.
Punctuates transitions (however, therefore) between clauses.
Chooses semicolons, dashes and subordination deliberately for effect.
Joins two ideas with because (or tells it from but) for an obvious link.
unless, if and although for a simple, clear relationship.
although at the start of a sentence; time relationships with tense (by the time).
Purpose and precaution (so that, in case).
Less common subordinators and positions (since meaning because, whereas).
Combines three or more ideas with subordination.
A stated fact in a very short, simple text.
A stated detail in a text of several paragraphs.
A stated detail with nearby distracting details.
A detail asked in different words from the text.
A precise detail in a dense or complex text.
An obvious feeling shown by an action (crying → sad).
A motive or feeling inferred from a clear sequence of actions.
Reasons and purposes inferred across a text.
Mixed or changing feelings, and a writer's attitude, from detail and dialogue.
Subtle, unstated motives and attitudes the reader must work out.
The topic of a very short text.
The gist or best title of a short story.
The main idea of one paragraph, not a detail.
The main idea of a multi-paragraph text, and of each paragraph.
The central idea or theme of a literary text; what each part does.
An implicit central claim stated only indirectly.
A reply that answers a simple question.
What a simple task needs (the main parts).
Every part of a multi-part task, with relevant content.
Content and language suited to a named reader.
Anticipates what the reader will need to know.
Sees that writing in one block needs paragraphs.
Paragraphs for the main parts, marked by changes of time or place.
Topic sentences and sensible paragraph length.
Each paragraph has one focus; breaks follow changes of focus.
Linking sentences between paragraphs.
Paragraphing that follows an argument's moves or is used for effect.
Finds and fixes basic errors in simple sentences (third-person -s).
Finds and fixes common errors (tense with a time marker, a/an, perfect with finished time).
Errors in more complex structures (agreement after pronouns, conditionals).
Rare slips in advanced structures (inversion, dangling participles, mixed conditionals).
Misspellings of very common words.
Misspellings of common longer words.
Misspellings of less common, frequently misspelled words.
Misspellings of rare words with double letters or silent letters.
Very common pairs and sets in short sentences (to/two/too, see/sea, sun/son).
there/their/they're and your/you're in everyday sentences.
its/it's: possessive against contraction, the most persistent common confusion.
Less common pairs and whose/who's (principal/principle, stationary/stationery).
Near-homophones that differ in one sound or in word class (accept/except, lose/loose, advice/advise).
Demanding pairs whose meanings are close (affect/effect, complement/compliment, discreet/discrete).
Adds a common prefix or suffix with no change at the join (unhappy, farmer, careless).
Keeps both letters where the prefix or suffix meets the same letter (misspell, unnatural, really).
-ful has one l, -ful + -ly keeps both l's (gratefully), -ment and the argue exception.
Chooses -able or -ible, which sound the same (comfortable, visible).
Chooses -tion, -sion or -ssion, and -ance or -ence (discussion, decision, difference).
Less common derived words, using roots and joins (irrelevant, occasionally, accommodate).
Classroom instruction words (underline, match, list).
Common cross-subject words recalled or matched in context (method, result, compare).
Tells similar instructions apart and answers what is asked (describe, explain, compare).
Abstract textbook words in their academic sense (factor, significant, evidence, evaluate).
Precise academic words for reasoning (hypothesis, implication, criteria, consequently).
un- and re- on familiar words (untie, reread, refill).
Works out and forms words with dis-, mis-, pre- and over-.
Chooses the right negative prefix: im-, il-, ir-, in-, un- (impossible, illegal, irregular).
Less common prefixes on familiar words (sub-, inter-).
Prefixes in abstract and academic words (counterproductive, semi-permanent, misconception).
Two everyday meanings of a very common word (a bat, to bat; a hand, give a hand).
Picks the meaning that fits the sentence for common words (light, record).
Less frequent everyday senses of familiar words (run a shop, do you mind).
Subject-specific meanings of familiar words (table, current, solution, mouth of a river).
Less obvious and figurative senses (a sharp decline, address a problem, a cold look).
Very common opposites (big/small, hot/cold, open/close).
A synonym or antonym for a common word in a sentence (begin/start, generous/selfish).
Synonyms and antonyms for less common words (narrow/wide, reluctant/unwilling).
Chooses the near-synonym that fits the sentence's meaning (exhausted, fragile, snapped).
Fine differences in meaning and attitude between near-synonyms (determined/stubborn, thrifty/stingy, glance/stare).
Very common fixed phrases (thank you very much, good morning, take a seat).
Common verb–noun pairs, including make and do (do homework, make a mistake, take a photo).
Verb–noun pairs that differ from a word-for-word translation (switch on the light, pay attention).
Adjective–noun and adverb collocations (heavy rain, strong argument, deeply sorry).
Less common and academic collocations (draw a conclusion, pose a question, bitterly disappointed).
Common simple similes read for their meaning, not literally (as cold as ice, runs like the wind).
Says what a simile or simple metaphor compares and which quality is shared.
Interprets less familiar metaphors and the feeling they create.
Extended or layered metaphors and how they shape a text's meaning.
Common phrasal verbs with literal meanings (sit down, get up).
Common idiomatic phrasal verbs (look after, give up, look for, find out).
Chooses between similar phrasal verbs with the same verb (put off, put up with, put out; call off).
Phrasal verbs with several meanings, chosen by context (pick up, make out, bring about).
Recognises when a general word (nice, good, thing) says less than a precise one.
Replaces a general word with a more precise verb, noun or adjective.
Chooses wording that is precise and suits the purpose (report, story, notice).
Chooses words for tone and effect, and notices advanced words used wrongly.
Regular plurals with -s and -es (cats, buses).
Consonant + y and common irregular plurals (babies, children, mice).
many with countable and much with uncountable nouns, typed.
Common uncountable nouns treated as singular, with no plural (information, advice, furniture, news).
Nouns used both ways and less common plurals (two coffees; criteria, phenomena).
Present simple for habits and regular past forms (walks, walked).
Common irregular past forms (went, bought).
The base form after did and didn't in questions and negatives.
Keeps tense consistent across a text; less common irregular forms (caught, chose, led).
Uncommon irregular forms (sought, wept, forbade).
can and can't for ability.
A modal takes the bare verb: no to, no -s (She can swim, not She can to swim).
must, should and may for obligation, advice and permission.
might and could for possibility, and could have for a missed possibility.
mustn't (not allowed) against don't have to (not necessary).
Deduction and nuance with past modals (must have, can't have, needn't have).
Understands who did the action in a simple passive with by.
Forms the present and past simple passive (is cleaned, was built).
Passives in other tenses and with modals (have been sold, will be announced, must be done).
Chooses the passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant; tells correct from broken passives.
Reporting passives (It is said that…, is believed to be…) and passives for focus in formal writing.
Understands zero-conditional sentences about routines and facts.
Forms first conditionals, with the present (not will) in the if-clause.
Forms second conditionals for imaginary situations (If I had…, I would…).
Forms third conditionals about the past (If we had left…, we would have…).
Mixed conditionals linking a past condition to a present result.
-er and -est on short adjectives (taller, smallest).
more and most with longer adjectives, and irregular forms (better, worst).
Spelling changes (bigger, happiest) and as … as.
less/fewer, far + comparative, the more …, the more …, and irregular further.
in, on and under for simple places.
at, in and on for common places (at the bus stop, in Chennai).
at, on and in for times (at seven, on Monday, in June).
since (a point in time) against for (a length of time).
by against until, and during against while.
Less common expressions (in time / on time, at the end / in the end).
Yes/no questions with be and can (Are you…? Can you…?).
Wh- questions with do, does and did, with the right word order.
Subject questions (Who phoned?) against object questions, and question tags.
Indirect and embedded questions, which keep statement word order.
Understands simple who and which clauses after a noun.
Joins two sentences with who, which or that, without repeating the pronoun.
whose and where, and commas around non-defining clauses.
Relative clauses with prepositions (in which, to whom) and reduced forms (the man sitting there).
Understands simple reported statements and works out the original words.
Reports statements with tense and pronoun changes.
Reports questions with if/whether and statement word order.
Reports commands and requests with told/asked + (not) to.
Reporting verbs with their patterns (denied taking, advised me to, suggested going).
Capitals at the start of a sentence and for I and names.
Capitals for days, months, festivals, places and languages.
Capitals for titles, organisations and proper adjectives, and none on common nouns.
Consistent conventions: inside quotations, titles before names, subjects against proper names.
A full stop at the end of a simple statement.
Question marks and exclamation marks, including in short dialogue.
No question mark on an indirect question; end marks in longer sentences.
End marks with quotations, inside or outside the quotation marks as the meaning requires.
Apostrophes in very common contractions (don't, I'm, isn't).
's for singular possession.
No apostrophe in plain plurals or ordinary verbs (mangoes, sells).
s' for plural possession, and its against it's.
Irregular plural possession (children's) and joint possession (Ravi and Sita's).
Recognises and writes simple complete sentences with a subject and a verb.
Finds and fixes obvious fragments, such as a because- or when-clause on its own.
Avoids -ing and which fragments in longer writing.
Recognises fragments used deliberately for effect, and where they are acceptable.
Joins two simple ideas with and or but, and chooses so for an obvious result.
Chooses and, but, or and so to show the right link.
yet, nor and paired forms (either … or, neither … nor), and avoids long chains of and.
Balances coordination and subordination for clarity and rhythm.
Understands and makes a sentence with a short describing phrase (the girl in the red dress).
Combines two sentences with who or which, without a repeated pronoun.
Combines with participle phrases without dangling them.
Embeds several ideas in one controlled sentence without overloading it.
first, then, next and finally to order events.
Common connectives for addition, contrast and result (also, however, so).
Chooses the connective that shows the exact relationship (as a result, for instance, despite this).
Uses transitions to guide a reader through an argument, including conceding a point.
Orders three or four events or steps in a very short text.
Orders events across a text of several paragraphs, using time words.
Orders events when the text tells them out of order (flashbacks, earlier stories).
Reconstructs complex timelines where the order of mention misleads.
Finds a cause stated with because or in the next sentence.
Links a cause and effect stated in different sentences or paragraphs.
Infers causes and effects that are not directly stated.
Distinguishes multiple causes, remedies from causes, and causes from coincidences.
Recognises the main event or topic of a short text.
Chooses the summary that covers the main points without small details or added opinion.
Identifies the key points of a multi-paragraph text and leaves out examples.
Condenses a text accurately, keeping the writer's line of thought or turning point.
Uses the title and headings to tell what a text is about and where to look.
Recognises sequence and description structures, and uses headings to find information.
Recognises compare-and-contrast, cause-and-effect and problem-and-solution structures and their signal words.
Explains how a text's structure supports its purpose.
Tells whether a text is a story, a letter or instructions.
Identifies the main purpose (inform, persuade, entertain, instruct), not just the topic.
Identifies the intended audience and how the language is chosen for it.
Explains mixed or hidden purposes, such as an advertisement written to look like news.
Tells a simple fact from a simple opinion.
Recognises opinion words (best, nicest, should, I think) in short texts.
Distinguishes opinions presented as facts, including claims with numbers or certainty.
Evaluates how a writer blends fact and opinion to persuade.
Recognises a reason or detail that adds to an idea, beyond a list.
Adds a reason or an example that is relevant to the idea.
Develops a main idea with relevant explanation and spots irrelevant detail.
Chooses the most telling detail and develops an argument in depth.
Puts events in a sensible order.
Orders ideas in a paragraph so a reader can follow them, starting with the main idea.
Orders points logically, with clear links between them.
Arranges content in the most effective order for the purpose and reader.
Recognises connected events and a sensible next event in a short story.
Recognises a story with a beginning, a middle and an ending that resolves it.
Recognises showing character and setting, and a clear problem and resolution.
Recognises control of pace, viewpoint and detail for effect.
States an opinion, and tells an opinion with a reason from one without.
Chooses relevant reasons for an opinion.
Supports a position with evidence and addresses the reader.
Answers counter-arguments and persuades through language without exaggerating.
Greetings and closings for a short message.
The main conventions of an informal email or notice (what, when, where; contact details).
Formal letter layout and register (subject line, salutation, Yours faithfully).
Well-judged functional texts for real purposes: complete, precise and suited to the reader.
Tells how to speak to a teacher from how to speak to a friend.
Changes wording for formal and informal readers.
Keeps a suitable register throughout, and spots wording that breaks it.
Adjusts register precisely for purpose, audience and effect (objective, warm, persuasive).
